text: SPECIAL SECTION: RESISTANCE Resistance Viewed from Different Perspectives One of the most dramatic shifts in the practice and theory of psychotherapy during the past two decades is the proliferation of many theoretical perspec- tives and the increased popularity of many treatment modalities. Although mainstream Freudian analysis is far from dead—its concepts and constructs continue to influence most contemporary therapists in many ways—self psychology, obiect relations, and numerous other "schools" are having a strong impact on us as we continue to define and redefine our roles in the therapeutic situation, and as we organize and reorganize our dynamic understanding of our patients. For many decades, long-term intensive treatment was the treatment of choice in most therapeutic settings, private and public. This situation has changed drastically, whereby short-term treatment is fast becoming the therapy of choice in many sectors. Managed care, a given in the practice of most clinicians, is certainly influencing this trend. As the unit of diagnostic understanding has become continually enlarged during the last twenty five years, the clinician's therapeutic armamentarium has also expanded. Many of us, in addition to treating individuals, are working with couples, families, groups, and larger units such as wards in a mental hospital. Different theoretical perspectives and modalities have their champions and denouncers. No sooner is a particular therapeutic modus operandi being praised, than the next day we hear that someone wants to bury it. Adherents to different points of view about theory and practice frequently appear like members of warring political parties who are out to defeat each other, rather than understand and learn from each. Often the different schools of thought and practice can also appear like religious cults that take the position that AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY, Vol. 50, No. 1, Winter 1996 29 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCnOTHERAPY anyone who does not endorse the law of the land is an infidel who deserves nothing but contempt and rejection! More heat than Hght is often generated when different theoreticat perspectives and practice modalities are discussed among colleagues. Conse- quently, many of us have wanted to discover a means of discussing therapeu- tic issues whereby the concepts and therapeutic practices would be the sole focus. This Special Section on Resistance is an attempt to implement this wish. One way that therapists from different persuasions can learn from, and about, each other is to choose one concept they all use and try to find out how the concept is explained and utilized by each. With very few exceptions, clinicians utilize the notion of resistance in their conceptualizations and therapeutic interventions. Therefore, in this Special Section we have the unique opportunity to see how recognized experts discuss and implement the notion of resistance in their practices. Although we leave it to you, dear reader, to discover the similarities and differences that emerge from the authors' presentations, a few observations are in order that may serve as an aid in organizing yourself for the upcoming ioumey. Despite the differing allegiances and biases, all of the writers in this Special Section endorse the concept of resistance and see its purposes similarly: 1. Each of the writers accepts the fact that all patients, sooner or later, experience dangers in the therapeutic situation and need to protect themselves. 2. Each of the writers denounces the practice of quickly trying "to get rid" of resistances, and instead, they all take the position that resistances must be understood and respected by therapist and patient. 3. Each of the writers accepts and utilizes the notion of counterresis- tance in his or her therapeutic work and believes that the patient's resistances cannot be resolved unless the therapist faces how he or she impedes the treatment. 4. Each of the writers has a humane attitude toward the therapy, wherein therapist and patient are two vulnerable human beings, both more human than otherwise. The overture to this presentation is by Mitchell May who presents a mainstream Freudian perspective. Although a believer that "drives" exist, he shows that so-called "drive theory" does not reject "objects" or "the self." A similar observation can be made regarding Peter Buckley's paper. 30 Resistance Viewed from Different Perspectives Though focusing sharply on the patient's interpersonal relationships (includ- ing the one with the therapist), the patient's instinctual wishes are not ignored. Combining traditional analytic theory with an object relations approach, Morton Kissen's work with married couples is intriguing. Applying the notion of projective identification, he shows how members of a marital dyad collude with each other and how the therapist can be drawn into this complex dynamic interplay. Like other authors in this section, Kissen shares with us how he uses his countertransference responses, particularly his anger, thera- peutically. Crayton Rowe, one of the country's leading self psychologists, in clear language tells us what Kohut is all about. He illustrates how self psychology's approach to resistances can help the patient truly feel that the therapist is an able ally. An outstanding teacher and author on group psychotherapy for many decades, Leslie Rosenthal shows us how some of the concepts of Modem Psychoanalysis can be profitably utilized in the group setting. Similarities and differences between group and individual resistances are clarified and the construct "joining the resistance" rather than breaking it is beautifully illustrated. The last paper in this Section is a very creative effort by Maxine Sigman. She helps us understand how very disturbed patients, most of them psy- chotic, handle resistances in a group situation. Her honest evaluation of her own counterresistances is heart warming and the results she gets in working with very sick patients are most encouraging. Our hope in presenting this Special Section is to encourage a dialogue among therapists. As we try patiently to understand and help each other resolve therapeutic dilemmas, maybe we can do the same with our patients. HERBERT S.
